[Discussion] Do you think a generic game title and overall hard searchability can be really bad for game's sales?
Are you thinking of any specific examples?

I do have trouble finding Black Ops 3 multiplayer specific content when I search for it; there's so much information about previous games, so that's all that shows up in searches until BO3 has been out for a while longer.

Unless the game is extensively marketed to be in the forefront of people's minds, having a generic title not only will hurt it's searchability, but also it's ability to stick in people's minds. They can't even begin to search for the game if they can't even recall what it's called. Unless there is a plan to spend a lot of money to get people talking, a generic title could be very bad on a game's sales.
Only if it doesn't go gangbusters in popularity.

Unless your a big name developer of tied to big name publisher then your fucked if people don't know about your product.

One of the many reasons that the Wii U failed is because so many people didn't know what it was or didn't know it existed. Everyone knew what a Wii was but the Wii U failed to differentiate itself and didn't even get the insta-buy that Nintendo can usually rely on.
Satellite Reign comes to mind. Great game in the spirit of the old Syndicate but imo a too generic title.
A name is very important. But sometimes games with shitty names, or not so spectacular names can succeed. Off the top of my head there's: Halo.

I don't think the uniqueness of a games title will have any effect on whether it sells well or not. As long as the spelling isn't so over the top that no one can figure it out, word of mouth and social media is what propels games above the noise of the internet. Think of any AAA title, indie game, or mobile app that you are aware of. Now think of how you heard about it. Prove me wrong if you can, but I'm not aware of any title that was marketed well but didn't sell because no one could find it on Google. I believe that if a game is actually good, not only will people find it, but they will help spread the word of it. A perfect example of this would be Psychonauts. When the game was released, it sold about 400k units, which is about what the new Tomb Raider has sold on XBone. Tomb Raider is basically a flop, and Psychonauts is considered one of the best platformer games ever made. Tomb Raider is a more searchable title than Psychonauts because most people probably can't spell the latter. So basically, Psychonauts has a difficult to spell name, was not critically acclaimed when released, and didn't sell terribly well but is highly regarded today. Tomb Raider is super easy to search, has previous games for context, had the best marketing available, was critically acclaimed, and ticked off every box that a AAA game should, and it still flopped (release date not withstanding).

Tl;dr: It doesn't matter if your game's title is searchable if the game itself is garbage. If the game is good, then weird titles and lack of provenance will not stop it from being great.

Edit for spelling.
Oh...reboots using the name overlapping the original title is also a bad trend since it also tampers the searchability of old games.

I guess. There is not a lot of smoke and mirrors around SEO anymore. It is not terribly difficult to get search results to show whatever product you want. There are entire companies that specialize in this service. My point was that SEO has nothing to do with whether a game is good or not. If a game is actually good, it will find its audience, in spite of its name, marketing, reviews, etc. If you are asking from the position of a dev who is trying to get a game out, then focus on making a good game. Let the people who specialize in SEO worry about your search rank. Putting lipstick on a pig will do nothing for the long term success of your game.
